name: Robert Hood and Mrs Hood
description: Impress thy brother, yet fret not thy mother. Robin's brother and mother are visiting, and Robin gets to choose the start day for each visitor. All days are numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. Visitors stay for $$$d$$$ continuous days, all of those $$$d$$$ days must be between day $$$1$$$ and $$$n$$$ inclusive. Robin has a total of $$$k$$$ risky 'jobs' planned. The $$$i$$$-th job takes place between days $$$l_i$$$ and $$$r_i$$$ inclusive, for $$$1 \le i \le k$$$. If a job takes place on any of the $$$d$$$ days, the visit overlaps with this job (the length of overlap is unimportant). Robin wants his brother's visit to overlap with the maximum number of distinct jobs , and his mother's the minimum. Find suitable start days for the visits of Robin's brother and mother. If there are multiple suitable days, choose the earliest one.
input_specification: The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1\leq t \leq 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case consists of three integers $$$n$$$, $$$d$$$, $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^5, 1 \le d, k \le n$$$) — the number of total days, duration of the visits, and the number of jobs. Then follow $$$k$$$ lines of each test case, each with two integers $$$l_i$$$ and $$$r_i$$$ ($$$1 \le l_i \le r_i \le n$$$) — the start and end day of each job. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output two integers, the best starting days of Robin's brother and mother respectively. Both visits must fit between day $$$1$$$ and $$$n$$$ inclusive.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2014D — Robert Hood and Mrs Hood [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
